knowledge_points.label: What large LMs share and where they differ
knowledge_points.statement: Across the dense LLM releases of 2024-2025, the core recipe is shared (pre-norm or other non-residual norm, RMSNorm, no biases, gated activations, serial blocks, 'LLaMA-like'), and the main remaining differences are position embeddings, activations and tokenization.

anchors.quote: Lots of architecture. Just in 2024-2025.. Over 19 new dense model releases, many of them with minor architecture tweaks..
High level view: Dominance of 'LLaMA-like' architectures. Trends over the years (QK-norm, Hybrid attention)
Differences: LayerNorm is in front of the block; Rotary position embeddings (RoPE); FF layers use SwiGLU, not ReLU; Linear layers (and layernorm) have no bias (constant) terms
Many aspects (arch, hparams) of transformers are in common across the big LMs. Major differences? Position embeddings, activations, tokenization
architectures are actually a very complex set of trade offs. ... it has to learn from data, so it has to generalize. ... It has to train efficiently on GPUs. ... And it has to not blow up.

in the early days of starting with a transformer until GPT-3 or so. ... There's a lot of experimentation that happens. ... And then Llama 2 comes out. ... last year, we saw really big differences or a trend towards architecture modifications that make training more stable.
We also see a lot of differences in how we handle context and how we handle position embeddings. ... Even tokenization, there's some differences.

provenance.filtering_note: p5-p6 are release-timeline figures (the '19 new dense model releases' count is in text, the list of models is a figure) and p9 is a table of models by year with their norm/attention choices that has no text layer beyond the two bullets quoted. p3 recaps the 2017 transformer (sines and cosines, ReLU, post-norm LayerNorm) and p4 the assignment-1 variant; those are the two ends of the comparison this deck walks through. The professor's stance on p2 ('the second best way is to try to learn from others' experience') is the method of the whole lecture: empirical survey, not derivation. Spoken evidence (5:43-7:13): the professor gives the three requirements every architecture must meet (generalize, train efficiently on GPUs, 'not blow up') as the reason the recipe is messy, and a history the slides only imply: open experimentation until about GPT-3, convergence on 'Llama 2 alikes', then last year a trend to stability modifications and this year to long-context variants. Why A1 uses pre-norm, RoPE and SwiGLU: 'we've copied a lot of this over from Llama, so did everyone else' (2:43). The 19 dense models are said aloud as last year's count; this year's releases are mostly mixtures of experts, deferred to the next lecture (3:32-4:13). His closing recap (1:28:39-1:28:58) names context handling, position embeddings and tokenization as the remaining differences, matching p67.

misconceptions.belief: Each new LLM release comes with a substantially new architecture.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p5 counts over 19 dense releases in 2024-2025 'many of them with minor architecture tweaks'; p9 calls the field dominated by LLaMA-like designs. The differences that survive (p67) are position embeddings, activations and tokenization.

knowledge_points.label: Pre-norm keeps the residual path clean
knowledge_points.statement: Pre-norm places LayerNorm inside each sub-block so the residual stream is never normalised; post-norm (original transformer, BERT) normalises after the add; almost all modern LMs use pre-norm because it gives nicer gradient propagation across layers, fewer gradient spikes, and tolerates larger learning rates (the original selling point was training without warmup).

anchors.quote: Set up LayerNorm so that it doesn't affect the main residual signal path (on the left) ... Almost all modern LMs use pre-norm (but BERT was post-norm) (One somewhat funny exception - OPT350M. I don't know why this is post-norm)
Gradient attenuation [Xiong 2020]   Gradient spikes [Salazar and Ngyuen]   Original stated advantage - removing warmup. Today - stability and larger LRs for large networks
Intuition - keep the good parts of residual connections. Observations - nicer gradient propagation, fewer spike
Basically, all modern language models push the layer norm outside of the residual stream. ... There is one funny exception, but it is OPT350M.
the early motivation for a lot of this was, when you train a transformer, you need to do a warm up. ... Actually, modern transformer training still does warm up as well.

keep your residual stream clean. ... that allows gradients to propagate in the backward pass, straight through this. ... if you do something like prenorm in blue at initialization, the gradient sizes remains the same
Stability and the ability to go deep are both very, very important for modern large language models.

provenance.filtering_note: The evidence on p11 (training curves from Nguyen & Salazar and Xiong) and the gradient-norm-per-layer plots on p12 are figures with no text layer; the slide text gives no numbers (no learning rates, no loss values). The mechanism is named ('gradient attenuation', 'gradient spikes') but not derived; Xiong 2020's argument that post-norm gradients at the last layers scale with the learning rate at initialization is not reproduced on the slides. Spoken evidence (9:57, 11:06-11:47): the principle behind p10 is said as a slogan, 'keep your residual stream clean': with pre-norm the input x reaches the output untouched, so at initialization the gradient sizes stay the same across layers, while post-norm rescales the gradient at every block. Caveat the slides lack: removing warmup was the original motivation, but 'modern transformer training still does warm up as well' (9:57), so pre-norm is kept for stability and depth (12:28-12:37), not to drop warmup. He suggests the consensus 'might partially be because Llama 2 did that' (19:07-19:16), and proposes calling post-norm 'residual norm' to avoid confusion with the newer non-residual post-norm (8:46-8:56).

misconceptions.belief: Pre-norm and post-norm differ only in where the normalisation layer is drawn; the trained model is equivalent.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In post-norm the normalisation sits on the residual stream, so every layer rescales the signal that skip connections are supposed to pass through unchanged; p12 attributes gradient attenuation and gradient spikes to exactly this, and p10 says the point of pre-norm is that it 'doesn't affect the main residual signal path'.

predict.q: Two 48-layer transformers are trained with the same large learning rate and no warmup, one post-norm and one pre-norm. According to slide 12, which one is the lecture expecting to diverge or need warmup?
predict.why: p12: removing warmup was the 'original stated advantage' of pre-norm, and today's reason is 'stability and larger LRs for large networks'. Post-norm shows gradient attenuation (Xiong) and gradient spikes (Nguyen & Salazar).
predict.targets_misconception: Pre-norm and post-norm differ only in where the normalisation layer is drawn; the trained model is equivalent.

transfer.q: You read a diagram of a transformer block where the LayerNorm box is drawn on the arrow that leaves the addition node and feeds the next block. Using slide 10's criterion, is this pre-norm or post-norm, and what single property of the residual path tells you?
transfer.answer: Post-norm: the norm is on the residual signal path itself (after the add), so the skip connection no longer carries the signal unchanged. Pre-norm would have the norm inside the branch, before attention/MLP, leaving the add-path untouched.
transfer.why: p10's rule is to place the norm 'so that it doesn't affect the main residual signal path'. Whatever sits on the add-path is by definition post-norm.

check.q: A 4-layer post-norm transformer has an attention and an MLP sub-block in every layer, each followed by its LayerNorm in the original-transformer position. How many normalisations does the signal on the residual path pass through between the embedding and the output of the last block? Type only the number.
check.why: Post-norm applies LN(x + F(x)) after every sub-block, so the residual signal itself is renormalised twice per layer: 2 × 4 = 8. In a pre-norm stack the norm sits inside each branch and the residual path passes through 0 of them until the final norm (p10, p12).
check.targets_misconception: Pre-norm and post-norm differ only in where the normalisation layer is drawn; the trained model is equivalent.
check.varies: counting norms on the residual path across a stack instead of classifying one diagram
check.invariant: a norm placed after the add sits on the residual signal path (post-norm); a norm inside the branch does not

retrieval.q: Name the two gradient pathologies the lecture attributes to post-norm and the paper each is credited to.
retrieval.answer: Gradient attenuation (Xiong 2020) and gradient spikes (Nguyen & Salazar 2019).

retrieval.q: What was the original stated advantage of pre-norm, and what is the reason given today?
retrieval.answer: Originally: training without warmup. Today: stability and tolerance of larger learning rates for large networks.

retrieval.q: Which two models does the lecture name as post-norm exceptions?
retrieval.answer: BERT and OPT-350M.

prompts.self_explain: Why would a normalisation that rescales the residual stream at every layer make gradients at early layers smaller (attenuation) in a deep post-norm stack?

presentations.notice: Switch from pre-norm to post-norm: only post-norm puts LN boxes on the straight residual line, and the count of norms on the stream climbs by 2 per layer, while pre-norm's stays at 0 however deep the stack.

knowledge_points.label: 'Double' norm: an extra post-norm outside the residual stream
knowledge_points.statement: Some recent models (Grok, Gemma 2) add a second normalisation on the sub-block output before it is added back, and OLMo 2 uses only this non-residual post-norm; the shared principle is that any norm may sit anywhere except on the residual stream itself.

anchors.quote: If putting LayerNorms in residual streams is bad.. Why not post-norm outside the stream? Recent models: Grok, Gemma 2. Olmo 2 only does non-residual post norm
Basically everyone does non-residual norm (often prenorm) ... Some people add a second norm outside the residual stream
Pre-vs-post norm: Everyone does non-residual norm (except OPT350M), likely with good reason.

if putting LayerNorms in residual streams is bad, why does LayerNorm have to be at the start? ... Many recent models, like Grok, or Gemma 2, or OLMo 2, have this structure where they've moved the LayerNorm after the computation.

if you have stability issues, you can sprinkle in LayerNorms everywhere. ... And that will generally improve stability. ... Every time people have encountered stability issues, they say, oh, but what if we just throw a LayerNorm into attention?

provenance.filtering_note: p13 shows block diagrams of the double-norm and OLMo-2 layouts as images; the text layer only names the models. No evidence (loss curves, stability numbers) is given for the double norm; p19 reports it as something 'some people' do. The lecture does not say why OLMo 2 dropped the pre-norm. Spoken evidence (13:25-13:47): the professor states the rule of thumb behind the double norm, 'if you have stability issues, you can sprinkle in LayerNorms everywhere', calls it 'ridiculous' yet 'proven right', and returns to it twice: QK-norm is the same move (1:09:48-1:10:04), and he lists the progression pre-norm, then norms after each sub-block, then norms on Q and K (1:11:43-1:11:56). It is a heuristic, not a result; no evidence is given for the double norm aloud either, and why OLMo 2 dropped the pre-norm is still not said.

prerequisites.note: p13 opens with 'If putting LayerNorms in residual streams is bad..', the conclusion of p10-p12.

misconceptions.belief: OLMo 2's 'post-norm' means it went back to the original transformer's post-norm.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p13 says OLMo 2 does 'non-residual post norm': the norm is applied to the sub-block output before the add, so the residual stream stays un-normalised, which is the opposite of the original post-norm on p3/p10.

predict.q: A block computes h = x + Norm_B(Attn(Norm_A(x))). Which of Norm_A / Norm_B sits on the residual stream itself, i.e. transforms the signal that the skip connection carries forward to the next block?
predict.why: Both norms act on the branch: Norm_A on the branch input (pre-norm), Norm_B on the branch output before the add (non-residual post-norm). x itself passes through untouched. This is the Grok/Gemma 2 'double norm' of p13.
predict.targets_misconception: OLMo 2's 'post-norm' means it went back to the original transformer's post-norm.

transfer.q: Write the OLMo 2 block update for the attention sub-block using the lecture's description on p13 (only a non-residual post-norm, no pre-norm).
transfer.answer: h = x + Norm(Attn(x)); the norm is applied to the sub-block output, not to x and not to the sum.
transfer.why: p13: 'Olmo 2 only does non-residual post norm'. The norm is outside the residual stream, so the add-path remains clean per p10's rule.

check.q: Which of these attention sub-block updates puts a normalisation on the residual stream itself, breaking the rule that all of OLMo 2, Gemma 2 and pre-norm models follow?
distractor_from: 'h = x + Norm(Attn(x))' <- misconception: 'OLMo 2's post-norm means it went back to the original transformer's post-norm.' (reads OLMo 2's non-residual post-norm as residual post-norm)
'h = x + Norm(Attn(Norm(x)))' <- plausible: two norms look like more interference, but both are inside the branch (Gemma 2 double norm)
'h = x + Attn(Norm(x))' <- control option: standard pre-norm
check.why: Only Norm(x + Attn(x)) transforms the sum that the skip connection carries forward; that is the original post-norm. The other three keep x untouched on the add path: pre-norm, OLMo 2's non-residual post-norm, and the Gemma 2 / Grok double norm (p13, p19).
check.targets_misconception: OLMo 2's 'post-norm' means it went back to the original transformer's post-norm.
check.varies: the learner identifies the violating update among four, instead of writing OLMo 2's update
check.invariant: a norm may sit anywhere except on the residual stream itself

retrieval.q: Which single placement of a norm layer does the lecture say every model except OPT-350M avoids?
retrieval.answer: On the residual stream (the original post-norm after the add); everyone does 'non-residual norm'.

retrieval.q: Name two models the lecture gives as examples of a second ('double') norm outside the residual stream.
retrieval.answer: Grok and Gemma 2 (OLMo 2 uses only the non-residual post-norm).

prompts.self_explain: Why does the lecture treat pre-norm and non-residual post-norm as members of the same family rather than opposites?

steps.do: Pre-norm: normalise a copy of x on its way into the branch.
steps.why: Norm_A reads x, but its output only feeds Attn; the x that the skip connection carries is not changed.

steps.do: The sub-block runs on the normalised copy.
steps.why: This is the branch: what it computes is added to the stream, it does not replace it.

steps.do: Second norm on the branch output, before the add: the Grok / Gemma 2 'double' norm of p13.
steps.why: It rescales only what the branch contributes, so the size of each block's update is controlled without touching x.

steps.do: Add to the residual. x reaches h unchanged, so neither norm sits on the residual stream.
steps.why: The test is whether the signal the skip connection carries passes through a norm; here only branch quantities do, which is what p19 calls non-residual norm.

presentations.notice: The double-norm (Grok, Gemma 2) and OLMo 2 wirings add LN boxes, but all of them sit on the branch: the residual-stream count stays 0, as with pre-norm. Only the original post-norm makes it nonzero.
listen for: the 'sprinkle LayerNorms everywhere' heuristic and its link to QK-norm later

knowledge_points.label: RMSNorm drops the mean and the bias; it wins on data movement, not FLOPs
knowledge_points.statement: RMSNorm computes y = x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * gamma, dropping LayerNorm's mean subtraction and bias beta; it performs as well as LayerNorm and is faster, but the saving is in data movement and parameters moved rather than FLOPs, because matrix multiplies dominate FLOPs and 'FLOPS are not runtime'.

anchors.quote: Original transformer: LayerNorm – normalizes ... the mean and variance across ... GPT3/2/1, OPT, GPT-J, BLOOM ... Many modern LMs: RMSNorm – does not ... subtract mean or add a bias term ... LLaMA-family, PaLM, Chinchilla, T5

Modern explanation - it's faster (and just as good). Fewer operations (no mean calculation). Fewer parameters (no bias term to store). Does this explanation make sense? Matrix multiplies are the vast majority of FLOPs (and memory) [Ivanov et al 2023]
Important lesson: FLOPS are not runtime! ... RMSNorm can still matter due to the importance of data movement. Left top ("43G") is FLOPS. Right top ("153") is the FLOP-to-memory ratio
RMSNorm runtime (and surprisingly, perf) gains have been seen in papers. Narang et al 2020
LayerNorm is more expressive than RMSNorm. ... But RMSNorm is nice, because in practice, there's really no expressiveness loss. ... But more importantly, it is faster.

something like 0.17% of the total floating point operations of our system. ... even though they're only 0.17% of the flops, depending on your workload and depending on the setup, can be up to 25% of the runtime.
the percent runtime in this case is quite extreme. ... This is like in the tiny models with matrices that don't really generally make sense in modern workloads
for teeny tiny transformer of a 200 million parameters, you get more steps per second. ... And in fact, you actually get better performance, which I don't think is something that you're guaranteed

provenance.filtering_note: The RMSNorm formula on p14 comes out of pdftotext as scattered symbols ('x', 'y = * gamma', '2', 'x 2+eps'); the quote reconstructs the stacked fraction. The Ivanov figure on p15-p16 that shows normalisation as a small share of FLOPs but a visible share of runtime is an image; the only numbers in the text are the two labels '43G' (FLOPs) and '153' (FLOP-to-memory ratio) and the slide does not say which operator they belong to. The Narang table on p17 (RMSNorm speed-up and loss) is a figure; the text claims only that gains 'have been seen'. The slide's RMSNorm formula divides by the l2 norm rather than the root-mean-square; the 1/d factor is absorbed by gamma up to a constant and is not discussed. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above: it says the only numbers in the text are '43G' and '153', but in class the professor reads the Ivanov figure aloud: normalisation is 'something like 0.17%' of FLOPs yet 'up to 25% of the runtime' (15:37-16:13), and then qualifies it as 'quite extreme', a tiny-model setting that does not reflect modern workloads (17:18-17:31). He reads the Narang table as more steps per second for a 200M-parameter model, plus a quality gain he says is not guaranteed (17:32-17:54). Also spoken: LayerNorm is more expressive, but RMSNorm loses nothing in practice (14:29-14:47).

external_prerequisites.note: p16's 'FLOP-to-memory ratio' label and the claim that data movement, not FLOPs, is what RMSNorm saves assume the learner can tell a memory-bound op from a compute-bound one.

misconceptions.belief: RMSNorm is faster because it removes a meaningful fraction of the model's FLOPs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p15 says matrix multiplies are 'the vast majority of FLOPs'; the norm's FLOPs are negligible. p16: 'FLOPS are not runtime' and the gain comes from data movement (one fewer pass over the activations, fewer parameters to move).

predict.q: Replacing LayerNorm by RMSNorm in a transformer changes two things in the forward pass. Which pair does slide 14 name?
choices: mean subtraction and the bias term beta are removed
variance scaling and the gain gamma are removed
mean subtraction and the gain gamma are removed
the epsilon and the bias term beta are removed
predict.answer: mean subtraction and the bias term beta are removed
predict.why: RMSNorm 'does not subtract mean or add a bias term'; it keeps the scale normalisation (by root-mean-square) and the learned gain gamma.
predict.targets_misconception: RMSNorm is faster because it removes a meaningful fraction of the model's FLOPs.

transfer.q: A profiler shows normalisation is under 1% of a model's FLOPs but about 10% of its step time. Using slides 15-16, which quantity explains the gap, and why would RMSNorm reduce the 10% more than the 1%?
transfer.answer: Data movement (memory traffic): normalisation is memory-bound, so its runtime is set by bytes moved, not FLOPs. RMSNorm skips the mean pass over the activations and stores no bias, cutting bytes moved; the FLOP share was already negligible.
transfer.why: p16: 'FLOPS are not runtime' and 'RMSNorm can still matter due to the importance of data movement'; p19: 'fewer parameters to move around, which saves on wallclock time'.

check.q: A training job moves to a new GPU with 2x the matmul FLOP/s but the same memory bandwidth. What happens to the fraction of step time spent in normalisation layers? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: up: normalisation is memory-bound, so its time is set by bytes moved and does not shrink, while the matmuls get faster; its share of the step grows.
check.why: p16: 'FLOPS are not runtime'. Norms are a tiny share of FLOPs but are limited by data movement; speeding up only the FLOP-bound part makes the memory-bound part a larger fraction. That is why RMSNorm's saving in bytes moved matters more than its saving in FLOPs (p15-p17).
check.targets_misconception: RMSNorm is faster because it removes a meaningful fraction of the model's FLOPs.
check.varies: the hardware changes instead of the norm; asks a direction rather than an explanation
check.invariant: normalisation runtime is set by memory traffic, not FLOPs

retrieval.q: Write the RMSNorm formula, naming the one learned parameter it keeps.
retrieval.answer: y = x / sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) * gamma (slide writes the denominator as the l2 norm); the only learned parameter is the gain gamma.

retrieval.q: What does the lecture say the 'modern explanation' for RMSNorm's speed gets wrong, and what is the corrected reason?
retrieval.answer: It credits fewer FLOPs, but matmuls dominate FLOPs; the real saving is data movement / parameters moved ('FLOPS are not runtime').

retrieval.q: Which model families does the lecture list under RMSNorm and which under LayerNorm?
retrieval.answer: RMSNorm: LLaMA family, PaLM, Chinchilla, T5. LayerNorm: GPT-1/2/3, OPT, GPT-J, BLOOM.

prompts.self_explain: Why can an operation that is a rounding error in the FLOP count still take a noticeable share of wall-clock time?

steps.do: Start from the original transformer's LayerNorm over the d_model entries of x.
steps.why: It normalises both the mean and the variance across d_model (p14) and has two learned vectors, γ and β.

steps.do: Drop the mean subtraction: divide by the root-mean-square sqrt(mean(x²) + ε) instead of the standard deviation.
steps.why: Without centring, the natural scale statistic is the RMS; this is p15's 'fewer operations (no mean calculation)'.

steps.do: Drop the bias β and keep the gain γ.
steps.why: p14: RMSNorm 'does not subtract mean or add a bias term'. γ stays, so one d_model vector of parameters remains instead of two (p15 'fewer parameters').

presentations.notice: Doubling matmul FLOP/s leaves the FLOP-share bar at 0.17% but raises the runtime share from 25% to 40%. Cutting the norm's FLOPs moves nothing; cutting its bytes does.
listen for: the two numbers the slide text lacks: about 0.17% of FLOPs, up to 25% of runtime

knowledge_points.label: Dropping bias terms from linear layers and norms
knowledge_points.statement: Most modern transformers remove the constant bias terms from linear layers (FFN(x) = sigma(x W1) W2 instead of sigma(x W1 + b1) W2 + b2) and from the norm, for the same reason as RMSNorm, namely memory and data movement, plus optimisation stability; the compute/parameter trade-off of a bias is 'not great'.

anchors.quote: Most modern transformers don't have bias terms. ... Most implementations (if they're not gated): ... Reasons: memory (similar to RMSnorm) and optimization stability
People more generally drop bias terms since the compute/param tradeoffs are not great.
Linear layers (and layernorm) have no bias (constant) terms

biased terms in transformers and neural networks are generally not that useful. ... most implementations actually just drop the biases entirely. ... not very arithmetically intense, but fairly memory intensive
where the bias terms can also induce stability issues ... But really, I think the primary reason these are dropped is just to simplify things from a systems perspective.
you can't really reason about this beforehand ... from a lot of experimentation and now, collectively acquired knowledge, we roughly that dropping the bias terms on both the linear and RMSNorm is OK

provenance.filtering_note: The 'Original Transformer' FFN with biases on p18 is an image; only the bias-free version survives in the text layer. No experiment is cited for 'optimization stability'; the claim is stated, not evidenced, on the slides. The lecture does not quantify the saving (a bias of size d_ff per layer is tiny relative to d_model x d_ff weights), which is exactly why the trade-off is described in terms of movement rather than count. Spoken evidence (18:35-18:49, 19:43-20:02): the professor ranks the two reasons. Stability is mentioned 'offhand'; 'the primary reason these are dropped is just to simplify things from a systems perspective'. He also says the choice cannot be reasoned out beforehand: that dropping biases is OK is 'collectively acquired knowledge' from many training runs, with 'no guarantee' (18:06).

prerequisites.note: p18 says the memory reason is 'similar to RMSnorm'.

misconceptions.belief: Biases are dropped because they add a large number of parameters.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A bias adds only d_ff (or d_model) parameters per layer against d_model x d_ff for the weight matrix; p18-p19 give memory/data-movement and optimisation stability, not parameter count, as the reasons, and call the compute/param trade-off 'not great' rather than large.

predict.q: A layer has W1 of shape 4096 x 16384 and a bias b1 of length 16384. What fraction of the layer's parameters is the bias? Give the answer as a percentage.
predict.why: 16384 / (4096 x 16384 + 16384) = 1/4097 = 0.024%. The bias is negligible as a parameter count, which is why the lecture's reason is movement and stability rather than size.
predict.targets_misconception: Biases are dropped because they add a large number of parameters.

transfer.q: A colleague proposes keeping the bias only in the LayerNorm ('it is just d_model numbers'). Which two reasons from slides 18-19 would the lecture give for dropping it anyway?
transfer.answer: Memory/data movement (one more tensor to load and store every step, same argument as RMSNorm) and optimisation stability; the compute/param trade-off of a bias is 'not great'.

'adding dropout to curb overfitting' <- plausible: treats bias removal as regularisation

knowledge_points.label: ReLU, GeLU and the gated (*GLU) feed-forward
knowledge_points.statement: A gated linear unit replaces the first half of the FFN, sigma(x W1), by sigma(x W1) ⊗ (x V), an entrywise product with an extra linear projection V; ReGLU uses ReLU, GeGLU uses GeLU (x Phi(x)), SwiGLU uses swish (x sigmoid(x)); gated models shrink d_ff by 2/3 to hold parameters constant, and Shazeer 2020 plus Narang et al. report fairly consistent gains, so GLUs are now consensus even though GPT-3 shows they are not necessary.

anchors.quote: ReLU ... Notable models: ... Original transformer, T5, ... Gopher, Chinchilla, OPT ... GeLU ... GPT1/2/3, GPTJ, GPT-Neox, BLOOM ... SwiGLU / GeGLU (next slide..) ... Llama, PaLM,T5 v1.1, most ... models post 2023

GLUs modify the 'first part' of a FF layer ... Instead of a linear + ReLU, augment the above with an (entrywise) linear term ... This gives the gated variant (ReGLU) – note that we have an extra parameter (V)
SwiGLU (swish is ... sigmoid ... LLaMa 1/2/3, PaLM, Mistral, ... OlMo, most models post 2023 ... Note: Gated models use smaller dimensions for the ... by 2/3
*GLU isn't necessary for a working model (see GPT3), but it's rare to see others.. Some outlier models.. Nemotron 340B (Squared ReLU). Evidence points towards somewhat consistent gains from Swi/GeGLU

even if you just want a ReLU, you can train a reasonably performant language model using just that activation. ... the only difference is this tiny divot at the bottom here, which really, for the most of the activation doesn't change anything but changes the gradients right near zero.
another thing that is often said in architecture design is that gating is often very helpful.

Generally, the Google folks have used GeGLU, so like the Gemma models, the T5 models are those. ... everything that's a Llama descendant uses a SwiGLU. ... amongst the gated units, doesn't really matter.

The original Noam Shazeer paper that proposed this had some very small deltas originally, but they're consistent deltas. ... this is a parameter matched comparison, because Noam Shazeer is always doing this 2/3 adjustment

provenance.filtering_note: The results on p24 (Shazeer 2020) and p25 (Narang et al.) are tables pasted as images; the slide text says only 'Yes, fairly consistently so' and 'other works corroborating'. No perplexity numbers are in the text layer. The p23 GeGLU formula is an image; only the swish definition is in text. The 2/3 rule is stated without derivation; the arithmetic (three matrices of size d_model x d_ff' versus two of d_model x d_ff gives d_ff' = 2/3 d_ff for equal parameters) is left to the learner and handled in the d_ff-ratio KP. Spoken evidence (25:01-25:40, 23:47-24:10): the professor reads the Shazeer table as 'very small deltas ... but consistent', backed by replicate runs with error bars, and stresses that the comparison is parameter-matched through the 2/3 adjustment. Which gate is used splits by lineage: GeGLU in Google models (Gemma, T5), SwiGLU in Llama descendants and PaLM, and 'amongst the gated units, doesn't really matter'. GeLU differs from ReLU only by 'this tiny divot' near zero, which changes the gradients there (21:09-21:23). Nemotron 340B uses squared ReLU, 'a crazy choice, but that works too' (26:47). Spoken slips (not imported): 'if you take a SwiGLU, which is x times a sigmoid, then you will get a SwiGLU' (23:33) calls swish 'SwiGLU' (p23 defines swish as x·sigmoid(x)). On the p29 table he says the GLU column holds 'almost always' GLUs 'with the exception of things like Falcon, which use a gated linear unit' (30:46), which contradicts itself: the exception is presumably a non-gated model.

prerequisites.note: p22 starts from the bias-free FFN of p18.

misconceptions.belief: SwiGLU is just a different nonlinearity swapped in for ReLU, with the same parameter count.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A GLU adds a third matrix V (p22: 'note that we have an extra parameter (V)') and multiplies its output entrywise with the activated branch; that is why gated models shrink d_ff by 2/3 (p23) to keep parameters comparable.

predict.q: A non-gated FFN has matrices W1 (d x f) and W2 (f x d). You switch to SwiGLU and keep f unchanged. By what factor does the FFN parameter count grow?
predict.why: SwiGLU adds V (d x f): three d x f matrices instead of two, a factor 3/2. Holding parameters fixed instead means shrinking f by 2/3, the rule on p23.
predict.targets_misconception: SwiGLU is just a different nonlinearity swapped in for ReLU, with the same parameter count.

transfer.q: Write FF_GeGLU(x) by analogy with slide 22's FF_ReGLU, using the GELU definition from slide 21.
transfer.answer: FF_GeGLU(x) = (GELU(x W1) ⊗ (x V)) W2, with GELU(u) = u Phi(u). Only the activation on the W1 branch changes; the gate x V stays linear.
transfer.why: p22's construction replaces the activation on the first branch and multiplies entrywise by the ungated linear term x V; GeGLU and SwiGLU differ from ReGLU only in that activation.

check.q: LLaMA-7B uses a SwiGLU FFN with d_model = 4096 and d_ff = 11008, and no biases. How many parameters does one FFN block have? Type only the number.
check.why: A gated FFN has three matrices, W1 and V (d_model × d_ff) and W2 (d_ff × d_model): 3 × 4096 × 11008 = 135,266,304. Counting only two matrices, as for a non-gated FFN, gives 9.0e7 (p22-p23).
check.targets_misconception: SwiGLU is just a different nonlinearity swapped in for ReLU, with the same parameter count.
check.varies: counts parameters of a real gated block instead of writing the GeGLU formula
check.invariant: a *GLU feed-forward adds a third projection V, so it has three d_model × d_ff matrices

retrieval.q: What is the swish function used in SwiGLU?
retrieval.answer: swish(x) = x * sigmoid(x).

retrieval.q: What extra parameter does a gated linear unit add to the feed-forward layer and how is it combined with the activated branch?
retrieval.answer: A third projection V; its output x V is multiplied entrywise (⊗) with the activated branch sigma(x W1).

retrieval.q: Which model does the lecture cite as proof that *GLU is not necessary, and which outlier uses squared ReLU?
retrieval.answer: GPT-3 (GeLU, no gate) works fine; Nemotron 340B uses squared ReLU.

prompts.self_explain: Why might multiplying the activated branch by a separate linear projection help more than simply choosing a smoother activation function?

steps.do: Start from the bias-free ReLU FFN: W_1 is d × d_ff, W_2 is d_ff × d.
steps.why: GLUs change only the 'first part', max(0, xW_1) (p22).

steps.do: Multiply the activated branch entrywise by a second, linear projection xV.
steps.why: The gate xV has no nonlinearity, so each hidden unit is scaled by a learned, input-dependent factor; V must be d × d_ff for the shapes to match.

steps.do: The result is ReGLU.
steps.why: W_2 still maps d_ff back to d; the only structural change is the extra parameter V that p22 points out.

steps.do: Parameters: 2·d·d_ff before, 3·d·d_ff after, a factor 3/2 at the same d_ff. Shrinking d_ff by 2/3 gives 3·d·(2/3)·d_ff = 2·d·d_ff again.
steps.why: That is p23's 'gated models use smaller dimensions for the d_ff by 2/3': it compares gated and ungated FFNs at equal parameters.

presentations.notice: Ticking the gate adds a third green FFN matrix: at the same d_ff the FFN grows to 1.5× its two-matrix size, while the attention segments do not move.
listen for: small but consistent gains, measured at equal parameter count

knowledge_points.label: Serial vs parallel transformer blocks
knowledge_points.statement: A standard block runs attention then the MLP in series; a parallel block (GPT-J, PaLM, GPT-NeoX, Cohere Command A, Falcon 2) computes both from the same normalised input and adds both to the residual, which lets the LayerNorm be shared and matrix multiplies be fused, but most models still use serial layers.

anchors.quote: Normal transformer blocks are serial - they compute attention, then the MLP. Could we parallelize the transformer block?

A few models (GPTJ, PaLM, GPT-NeoX) do parallel layers. Originally in GPT-J. If implemented right, LayerNorm can be shared, and matrix multiplies can be fused. Recent Models: Cohere Command A, Falcon 2 11B, Command R+
Serial vs parallel layers: Most models now use serial layers
If you're very systems-minded, you might say, well, this introduces a bottleneck. ... I have to wait for the computation of one to do the other.

This has been an approach that has really fallen out of popularity over the past, I think, two years, I think mainly because optimization of the serial form has gotten sufficiently good ... Effectively, you can think about it, as you've lost half of your depth.

if you read the original PaLM paper, I think they're very confident about the use of parallel layers, like no performance drop, 15% systems utilization improvement. ... a lot of the later Google models have stopped using this

provenance.filtering_note: The serial and parallel block equations on p27-p28 are images; the text layer has no formula, so the statement's y = x + Attn(LN(x)) + MLP(LN(x)) form is the author's reconstruction from PaLM §2. The lecture gives no quality numbers (PaLM reports a small degradation at small scale that vanishes at 62B; not on the slides) and does not say why most models stayed serial. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above: it says the lecture 'does not say why most models stayed serial', but the professor does: optimisation of the serial block 'has gotten sufficiently good' that the systems gain is not worth the representational cost, and 'you've lost half of your depth' (28:59-29:23). In the Q&A (40:50-41:25) he quotes PaLM as 'no performance drop, 15% systems utilization improvement', reads later Google models abandoning parallel layers as 'an implicit signal that actually, there might be some losses', and says no controlled ablation exists. 'No performance drop' simplifies PaLM, which reports a small degradation at 8B that disappears at 62B (paper, not slides).

prerequisites.note: Sharing one LayerNorm between the two branches only makes sense in a pre-norm block.

misconceptions.belief: Parallel layers are the modern default because they are faster.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p29: 'Most models now use serial layers'. The parallel form appears in a short list (GPT-J, PaLM, GPT-NeoX, Command A, Falcon 2) and the lecture offers the fusion/shared-norm benefit as an 'if implemented right' possibility, not a consensus.

predict.q: In a parallel block, how many LayerNorm applications are needed per block if 'implemented right' (slide 28), compared to a serial pre-norm block?
predict.why: Both branches of a parallel block read the same normalised input, so the LayerNorm 'can be shared'; a serial block normalises once before attention and once before the MLP.
predict.targets_misconception: Parallel layers are the modern default because they are faster.

transfer.q: Write the residual update of a parallel pre-norm block in one line, then say what the MLP's input is in the serial block that the parallel one gives up.
transfer.answer: y = x + Attn(LN(x)) + MLP(LN(x)). In the serial block the MLP sees x + Attn(LN(x)), i.e. the attention output of the same layer; the parallel block's MLP cannot use it.
transfer.why: p27: serial computes attention 'then the MLP'; p28: parallel computes both from the shared normalised input, which is what allows the shared norm and fused matmuls.

check.q: Compared with a serial pre-norm block, what can the MLP in a parallel block NOT do?
distractor_from: 'share its norm with attention' <- reverses the trade-off: a shared norm is what parallel blocks gain (p28)
'fuse its matmul with attention's' <- same reversal: fused matmuls are the parallel block's selling point
'use the previous layer's output' <- plausible: both blocks read the previous layer's residual stream
check.why: In a parallel block y = x + Attn(LN(x)) + MLP(LN(x)), both branches read the same input x, so the MLP never sees this layer's attention result. The serial MLP reads x + Attn(LN(x)) (p27-p28).
check.varies: the learner picks the lost capability from a list that includes the parallel block's gains
check.invariant: parallel blocks compute attention and MLP from the same input; serial blocks feed the attention output to the MLP

retrieval.q: Which model introduced parallel transformer layers, per the lecture?
retrieval.answer: GPT-J.

retrieval.q: What two implementation savings does the lecture attribute to parallel layers?
retrieval.answer: The LayerNorm can be shared between the branches, and the matrix multiplies (attention and MLP input projections) can be fused.

prompts.self_explain: Why can the attention and MLP input projections be fused into one matmul only in the parallel block?

presentations.notice: In the parallel wiring one LN feeds both Attn and MLP (1 norm per layer instead of 2), and the readout's 'MLP reads this layer's attention output' turns to no.
listen for: the two reasons parallel blocks faded: serial blocks got fast enough, and parallel halves effective depth

knowledge_points.label: Four families of position embeddings, and why RoPE won
knowledge_points.statement: Position information enters a transformer as sinusoidal additive vectors (original), learned absolute vectors added to the token embedding (GPT-1/2/3, OPT), relative terms added inside the attention computation (T5, Gopher, Chinchilla), or RoPE, which rotates queries and keys so that the attention score depends only on i - j (GPT-J, PaLM, LLaMA, most 2024+ models).

anchors.quote: Sine embeddings: add sines and cosines that enable localization ... Absolute embeddings: add a position vector to the embedding ... GPT1/2/3, OPT ... Relative embeddings: add a vector to the attention computation ... T5, Gopher, Chinchilla ... Rope embeddings ... GPTJ, PaLM, LLaMA

a relative position embedding should be some ... the attention function only gets to depend on the relative position (i-j) ... Sine: Has various cross-terms that are not relative ... Absolute: obviously not relative ... Relative embeddings: ... is not an inner product
Difference with sine embeddings - not additive, no cross terms
Note: embedding at each attention operation to enforce position invariance
attention is positionally independent. ... They're just inner products, so you can just shuffle them. ... The original transformer had sine and cosine embeddings, a Fourier transform intuition
you're adding a vector to the attention computation itself. ... So if you're three positions off, the attention matrix gets a different offset added to it.

Sine is not relative, because it has these absolute cross terms that are not relative. ... relative embeddings, technically, these are relative, but they're not embeddings, because they're just adding to the attention matrix.
proportional RoPE or p-RoPE, which is a really strange way to just say that the only thing they rotate is the first two coordinates
the low frequency parts just aren't rotating very much. ... And so you can drop them if you're really strapped for of extra space. ... this is really an optimization for teeny tiny models

provenance.filtering_note: This KP covers only the taxonomy on p30 and the one-line verdicts on p31/p34/p35. The RoPE derivation (p32 'we know that' rotation example, p33 pairing coordinates, p34 the actual math, p35 the code) is covered by the rope paper thread and not duplicated here; the p33 remark 'Gemma 4 alternative: just first 2' (rotate only a prefix of the coordinates) is noted but is a figure caption without explanation. The sine cross-term expansion on p31 is partially an image; the text layer shows only the first terms. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above: it calls the p33 remark 'Gemma 4 alternative: just first 2' a caption without explanation, but the professor names it ('proportional RoPE or p-RoPE', rotating only the first coordinates, 37:15-37:31) and, in the Q&A, gives the reason: low-frequency pairs barely rotate, so they can be dropped, 'an optimization for teeny tiny models' (41:35-42:02). Which pairs Gemma 4 keeps is not settled by the audio. Also spoken: why position must be added at all (attention is a set of inner products, so shuffling tokens changes nothing, 31:27-31:36), why each earlier scheme fails the relative criterion (33:50-34:11), and that additive relative schemes 'can't be factorized as a product', which he calls 'more of an aesthetic problem' since such schemes 'do reasonably well' (43:01-43:30). Spoken slip (42:13), not imported: answering a question he says relative position is 'applied both to the keys and values'; RoPE is applied to queries and keys, as he said at 38:31 and as p35 shows.

prerequisites.note: p67 names position embeddings as one of the three remaining differences.

external_prerequisites.note: p31's <f(x,i), f(y,j)> = g(x, y, i-j) is the RoPE paper's goal equation.
Why a rotation makes the score depend only on i - j.
p35: RoPE is applied at every attention operation, not once at the input.

misconceptions.belief: Sinusoidal embeddings already give relative-position attention because sin/cos of (i + k) are linear in sin/cos of i.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p31: the inner product <v_x + PE_i, v_y + PE_j> expands into cross-terms <v_x, PE_j> and <PE_i, v_y> that depend on absolute position; only the PE-PE term is relative. RoPE is multiplicative and has 'no cross terms' (p34).

predict.q: Expand <v_x + PE_i, v_y + PE_j> for sinusoidal PE (whose inner product <PE_i, PE_j> depends only on i - j). How many of the four terms depend on an absolute position (i or j alone) rather than only on i - j?
predict.why: <v_x, v_y> has no position; <PE_i, PE_j> depends only on i - j for sinusoids; the two cross-terms <v_x, PE_j> and <PE_i, v_y> each depend on an absolute position. These are the 'various cross-terms that are not relative' of p31.
predict.targets_misconception: Sinusoidal embeddings already give relative-position attention because sin/cos of (i + k) are linear in sin/cos of i.

transfer.q: A model adds a learned vector u_i to the token embedding at the input and nowhere else. Classify it on slide 30's taxonomy and say which of the p31 criteria it fails.
transfer.answer: Absolute embedding (GPT-style). It fails relativity outright: the score depends on i and j separately ('obviously not relative'), and position enters only once at the input rather than at each attention operation.
transfer.why: p30 defines absolute embeddings as Embed(x,i) = v_x + u_i; p31 lists them as not relative; p35 notes RoPE is applied at every attention layer.

check.q: A model applies RoPE to queries and keys in every attention layer, and also adds a learned absolute vector u_i to the token embedding at the input. Does its attention score depend only on i − j?
choices: yes: RoPE makes every score depend only on i − j
no: it also depends on i and j separately
no: it depends on neither i nor j
check.answer: no: it also depends on i and j separately
distractor_from: 'yes: RoPE makes every score depend only on i − j' <- plausible: treats RoPE as making attention relative no matter what else enters the residual stream
'no: it depends on neither i nor j' <- plausible: assumes the two position signals cancel
check.why: RoPE's rotation keeps the q·k term a function of i − j only for the content it rotates, but u_i is part of that content: q_i = W_q(v_x + u_i), so the score contains terms such as <W_q u_i, R_{j−i} W_k v_y> that depend on i alone. Anything added at the input leaves absolute cross terms, which is why RoPE models drop the absolute embedding.
check.varies: RoPE in every layer plus an absolute vector at the input, instead of an input-only sinusoid
check.invariant: any position vector added at the input leaves cross terms that depend on absolute position

retrieval.q: List the four position-embedding families the lecture names, with one example model each.
retrieval.answer: Sinusoidal (original transformer); learned absolute (GPT-1/2/3, OPT); relative added to attention (T5, Gopher, Chinchilla); RoPE (GPT-J, PaLM, LLaMA, most 2024+ models).

retrieval.q: State the property a relative position embedding should satisfy, as an equation.
retrieval.answer: <f(x, i), f(y, j)> = g(x, y, i - j): the attention score depends on positions only through i - j.

retrieval.q: Where in the network is RoPE applied, and why?
retrieval.answer: At each attention operation (on queries and keys), to enforce position invariance at every layer rather than only at the input.

prompts.self_explain: Why does adding position to the token embedding (additive) necessarily create cross-terms, while rotating queries and keys (multiplicative) does not?

presentations.notice: listen for: why sine, absolute and additive relative schemes each fail the 'inner product depends only on i - j' test

knowledge_points.label: d_ff = 4 d_model, or 8/3 d_model for gated FFNs
knowledge_points.statement: Almost all transformers set d_ff = 4 d_model; gated (GLU) models scale this by 2/3 to d_ff = 8/3 d_model ≈ 2.67 d_model so the three FFN matrices hold the same parameters as two, with observed ratios 2.5-4 (PaLM 4, Mistral/LLaMA-2 3.5, LLaMA/Qwen/DeepSeek ≈2.68, T5 v1.1 2.5); T5 11B's 64x (d_ff = 65,536, d_model = 1024) and Gemma 2's 8x are the exceptions, and Kaplan 2020 finds a near-optimal basin anywhere between 1 and 10.

anchors.quote: There are two dimensions that are relevant – the feedforward dim ... and model dim ... What should their relationship be? ... This is almost always true. There's just a few exceptions.

Remember that GLU variants scale down by 2/3 rd. This means most GLU variants have ... This is mostly what happens. ... PaLM 4 ... Mistral 7B 3.5 ... LLaMA-2 70B 3.5 ... LLaMA 70B 2.68 ... Qwen 14B 2.67 ... DeepSeek 67B 2.68 ... Yi 34B 2.85 ... T5 v1.1 2.5

One exception is T5 [Raffel et al 2020] which has some very bold settings. ... In particular, for the 11B model, they set ... 65,536 ... 1024 ... For an astounding 64-times multiplier. ... Other, recent exceptions – Gemma 2 (8x), SmolLM/Gemma 3/Gemma 4 (4x, GLU)
Empirically, there's a basin between 1-10 where this hyperparameter is near-optimal [Kaplan+ 2020]
T5 has a follow-up model (T5 v1.1) that is 'improved' and uses a much more standard 2.5 multiplier on GeGLU, so the 64-times multiplier is likely suboptimal.
it should maybe be four times your hidden dimension. ... And this is a rule of thumb that works remarkably well.
this another systems-based argument. ... the bigger my matrix multiplies, the more efficient I can keep my hardware.

there's a basin, where you start at about one, and you end about maybe 10, where this hyperparameter is pretty good and very, very flat. ... if you get it really wrong, you get above 10 to 100 or something like that, then your loss starts really shooting up
T5 was a fine model or the version 1 T5 was a fine model. ... And so even radical choices can technically work, but it's probably going to be compute-inefficient.

provenance.filtering_note: The '8/3' on p38 is a stacked fraction in the layout (digits '8' and '3' on separate lines); the quote reconstructs it. The Kaplan basin figure on p40 carries the loss-vs-ratio curve; the only number in text is the '1-10' range. The slides never derive why 2/3: with three d_model x d_ff' matrices (W1, V, W2) versus two d_model x d_ff, equal parameters needs 3 d_ff' = 2 d_ff, i.e. d_ff' = 2/3 d_ff = 8/3 d_model; this is left implicit and the interactive here makes the learner compute it. Mistral/LLaMA-2 at 3.5 are 'slightly larger' than 8/3 by the slide's own admission (SwiGLU with d_ff = 3.5 d_model carries 1.3x the FFN parameters of a 4x ReLU block). Spoken evidence (47:17-47:36, 48:25-49:20): the professor gives T5's reason for the 64x multiplier, a systems argument ('the bigger my matrix multiplies, the more efficient I can keep my hardware'), and reads the Kaplan figure beyond the slide's '1-10': flat inside the basin, loss 'really shooting up' past 10 toward 100. His verdict: 'even radical choices can technically work, but it's probably going to be compute-inefficient'. The reason he gives for LLaMA-2's 3.5 (efficient attention heads) is a separate spoken-only KP, gqa-frees-ffn-budget.

prerequisites.note: p38 'Remember that GLU variants scale down by 2/3 rd' refers back to p23.

external_prerequisites.note: Counting FFN parameters as products of matrix dimensions.

misconceptions.belief: Gated models use d_ff = 8/3 d_model because a smaller hidden width works better with a gate.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The 2/3 factor is a parameter-matching convention: three matrices of width 8/3 d_model have the same parameter count (8 d_model^2) as two of width 4 d_model. p38 derives it from 'GLU variants scale down by 2/3', not from any quality result; the quality evidence (p40, Kaplan) says anything between 1x and 10x is near-optimal.

predict.q: d_model = 4096. A ReLU FFN uses d_ff = 4 d_model. A SwiGLU FFN wants the same number of FFN parameters. What d_ff should it use?
predict.why: ReLU FFN: 2 x 4096 x 16384 = 134M. SwiGLU has three matrices, so 3 x 4096 x d_ff = 134M gives d_ff = 2/3 x 16384 = 10923 ≈ 8/3 x 4096. In practice this is rounded to a multiple of 256 (LLaMA-7B uses 11008).
predict.targets_misconception: Gated models use d_ff = 8/3 d_model because a smaller hidden width works better with a gate.

transfer.q: Mistral 7B uses SwiGLU with d_ff / d_model = 3.5 (slide 38). Compared with a ReLU block at the 4x rule, by what factor are Mistral's FFN parameters larger? Then say whether slide 40's evidence suggests this hurts.
transfer.answer: 3 x 3.5 / (2 x 4) = 1.31x more FFN parameters. Slide 40 says the near-optimal basin spans ratios 1-10, so 3.5 is well inside it; the lecture only notes these models are 'slightly larger'.
transfer.why: Parameter count scales with (number of matrices) x ratio; the Kaplan basin is the lecture's only quality evidence and it is flat over that range.

check.q: T5 v1.1 uses a gated (GeGLU) FFN with d_ff / d_model = 2.5. Compared with a non-gated ReLU FFN at the 4x rule with the same d_model, what is the ratio of their FFN parameter counts (gated / ReLU)? Type only the number.
check.why: Gated: 3 matrices × 2.5 d² = 7.5 d². ReLU: 2 × 4 d² = 8 d². Ratio 7.5 / 8 ≈ 0.94, slightly fewer parameters than the 8/3 rule would give (1.0). Parameter count is (number of matrices) × ratio (p37-p38).
check.varies: a ratio below 8/3 instead of above it

knowledge_points.label: Shared K/V heads free parameters for a wider FFN (LLaMA-2 and Mistral at 3.5)
knowledge_points.statement: Sharing key/value heads (GQA/MQA) shrinks a layer's attention projections from 4 d_model^2 to (2 + 2g/h) d_model^2 for h query heads and g key/value heads, and the professor gives this as the reason LLaMA-2 multiplies the gated ratio 8/3 by 'an arbitrary 1.33' to about 3.5: the parameters saved in attention are spent on the MLP (slide p38 lists the GQA models LLaMA-2 70B and Mistral 7B at 3.5).

anchors.quote: the Llama 2 folks decided, well, we actually have very efficient attention heads with MQA, which I'll talk about later. ... because of that, we can multiply this ratio by an arbitrary 1.33. ... And we'll get roughly 3.5. ... which essentially emphasizes the MLPs a little bit more.
if you actually look through all the papers, you'll find either 2.6-ish or 3.5 for GLUs, or 4 if you're doing non-GLU models.
Models are roughly in this range, though PaLM, LLaMA2 and Mistral are slightly larger

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only for the reason. Slide p38 lists Mistral 7B and LLaMA-2 70B at 3.5 and calls them 'slightly larger' without saying why. The reason (efficient attention heads let the ratio be multiplied by 'an arbitrary 1.33', which 'emphasizes the MLPs') is only in the audio (46:01-46:28). Imprecision, not imported: he says 'MQA', but LLaMA-2 70B and Mistral 7B use grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads (LLaMA-2 and Mistral papers, not the slides). LLaMA-2 7B and 13B keep full multi-head attention and use about 2.7 (11008/4096, 13824/5120), which fits his reading. 3.5 / (8/3) = 1.31, rounded aloud to 1.33. The parameter arithmetic, (2 + 2g/h) d^2 for attention and 3 x ratio x d^2 for a gated FFN, and the equal-parameter framing in the prompts are the author's. The professor says only that the budget goes to the MLPs, and the real models are not exactly parameter-matched (LLaMA-2 70B: 12.75 d^2 per layer against 12 d^2 for MHA with SwiGLU at 8/3). GQA itself is taught at 1:15-1:23 (mqa-gqa-kv-cache).

misconceptions.why_wrong: The K and V projections shrink with the number of KV heads (each is d_model x g·d_head), so a GQA layer has fewer attention parameters. That saved budget is what LLaMA-2 moved into the FFN.

Following the professor's LLaMA-2 argument, where does the saved budget go, and to what d_ff/d_model can the SwiGLU FFN grow?

transfer.why: Parameters saved in the K/V projections can be re-spent where they buy capacity. A gated FFN has three d x d_ff matrices, so each extra 3 d^2 raises the ratio by 1. The trade is K/V expressiveness (the MQA quality hit on p63) for MLP width.

retrieval.answer: 2 + 2g/h: Q and O are d x d, and K and V are d x (g/h)d each.

knowledge_points.label: head_dim x num_heads = d_model is a convention, not a constraint
knowledge_points.statement: Most models set head_dim x num_heads equal to d_model (ratio 1: GPT-3 96 x 128 = 12288, LLaMA-2 64 x 128 = 8192), but nothing forces it: T5 used 128 x 128 = 16384 against d_model 1024 (ratio 16), LaMDA ratio 2, Qwen 3.5 27B 1.2, PaLM 48 x 258 = 12384 against 18432 (ratio 0.67, printed inverted as 1.48), and the lecture says this rule has 'low to no validation'.

anchors.quote: Head-dim*num-heads to model-dim ratio. ... This doesn't have to be true: we can have head-dimensions > model-dim / num-heads. But most models do follow this guideline

Num heads / Head dim / Model dim / Ratio: GPT3 96 128 12288 1; T5 128 128 1024 16; T5 v1.1 64 64 4096 1; LaMDA 128 128 8192 2; PaLM 48 258 18432 1.48; LLaMA2 64 128 8192 1; Qwen 3.5 (27B) 24 256 5120 1.2. Most models have ratios around 1 - notable exceptions by some google models.
Head dim: Head dim*Num head = D model is standard - but low to no validation
the dimension of each head is d over h. So you multiply the two and you get d. ... For some reason, this is the rule of thumb. ... Of course, this doesn't have to be true.
I think this is yet another forgiving hyperparameter. ... There's a couple ablations that people have done. ... There's, once again, a pretty wide basin around one that you can get away with.

provenance.filtering_note: The '224n slide' reminder on p42 is an image. The ratio column on p43 is num_heads x head_dim / d_model for every row except PaLM, where 1.48 = 18432 / (48 x 258) is the inverse (PaLM's paper does use head dim 258 and 48 heads); PaLM's ratio on the slide's own convention is 0.67, i.e. the only listed model whose attention width is smaller than d_model. The lecture does not explain what changes when the ratio differs from 1 (the Q/K/V/O projections become d_model x (h x k) rectangles and attention FLOPs scale with h x k rather than d_model). Spoken evidence (51:13-51:28): aloud the professor calls this 'yet another forgiving hyperparameter' with 'a couple ablations' showing 'a pretty wide basin around one'. That is milder than p51's 'low to no validation'; neither the slides nor the audio name the ablations. The statement keeps the slide's wording because he does not retract it.

knowledge_points.label: Aspect ratio d_model / n_layers: wide range, set by systems concerns
knowledge_points.statement: Models cluster at d_model / n_layers between roughly 100 and 200 (GPT-3/OPT/Mistral/Qwen/OLMo 3 at 128, LLaMA at 102, PaLM 540B at 156, BLOOM at 205), with Gemma 3 (87), Gemma 4 (61) and T5 11B (43; slide p44 prints 33, which is GPT-2's 1600/48, while p51 lists 43) deeper; Kaplan 2020 and Tay 2021 show loss is insensitive over a wide range, so the choice is dictated by systems concerns since very deep models are harder to parallelise and have higher latency.

anchors.quote: Should my model be deep or wide? How deep and how wide? ... Most models are surprisingly consistent on this one too! ... BLOOM 205 ... T5 v1.1 171 ... PaLM (540B) 156 ... GPT3/OPT/Mistral/Qwen 128 ... /OLMo 3 ... LLaMA / LLaMA2 102 ... Gemma 3 87 ... Gemma 4 61 ... T5 (11B) 33 ... Sweet spot?
Extremely deep models are harder to parallelize and have higher latency [Tay et al 2021]
Aspect ratio: Wide range of 'good' values (100-200). Systems concerns dictate the value

when you scale models up or down, the way you usually do that is you fix an aspect ratio, like how wide your model is versus how deep it is. ... So the aspect ratio, in some sense, controls the entire depth to width trade off as you make models bigger.

Once you start cutting up your layers depth-wise, you have very serious issues in parallelization. ... Pipeline parallel, which is what this is called ... Whereas width is much easier to parallelize. ... Tensor parallel is what it's called.
as you sweep the depth to width trade offs, you find that really, the only thing that matters, in some sense, is flops.

provenance.filtering_note: p45 and p46 are figures (Tay's depth-vs-width downstream plots and Kaplan's aspect-ratio loss curves); their numbers are not in the text. The 'Sweet spot?' label on p44 sits beside the 128 row in the layout. The lecture does not quantify 'harder to parallelize' (pipeline-parallel bubbles grow with depth; latency scales with the number of sequential layers) and states it as a citation to Tay. Spoken evidence, which partly corrects the note above: the lecture still does not quantify 'harder to parallelize', but the professor names the mechanism: splitting a model by depth needs pipeline parallelism, 'something that most people really, really do not want to deal with', while width splits easily with tensor parallelism (53:00-53:29; details deferred to the systems lectures). He adds why the ratio matters: models are scaled up at a fixed aspect ratio, so it sets the whole depth/width trade-off (51:37-51:57), and he reads the Tay figure as 'the only thing that matters, in some sense, is flops' (54:36-54:47). He rounds the band to 'about 100' (52:29) where p44/p51 say 100-200 with most models at 128.

misconceptions.belief: There is a single optimal depth/width ratio that the scaling-law papers pin down.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p51: there is a 'wide range of good values (100-200)' and 'systems concerns dictate the value'; the loss curves in Kaplan and Tay are flat over that range, so the deciding factors are parallelism and latency, not loss.

knowledge_points.label: Vocabulary size: 30-50k monolingual, 100-250k multilingual/production
knowledge_points.statement: Monolingual models use vocabularies of about 30-50k tokens (GPT-2/3 50257, T5 32128, LLaMA 32000, original transformer 37000) while multilingual and production systems use 100-250k (GPT-4 100276, DeepSeek 100000, Qwen 152064, mT5 250000, PaLM 256000, Gemma 4 262144); monolingual vocabularies do not need to be huge, multilingual ones do.

anchors.quote: Monolingual models – 30-50k vocab ... Multilingual / production systems 100-250k ... Original 37000 ... mT5 250000 ... PaLM 256000 ... GPT2/3 50257 ... Gemma 4 262144 ... LLaMA 32000 ... Qwen 15B 152064 ... Monolingual vocabs don't need to be huge, but multilingual ones do
you had these much smaller vocab sizes, in the 30,000 range. ... All of these have much, much larger vocab sizes. ... these are roughly in the 100,000 to 200,000 vocab range.
The multilingual models really do need much larger vocab to cover the whole space. ... There have been scaling law studies, showing that the bigger your model, the larger the vocab it can handle.
if you're tokenizing your images and things like that, then you need to have many more tokens to account for those. ... they'll have a different image tokenizer with its own vocab

provenance.filtering_note: The slide gives counts only; it does not say what a larger vocabulary costs (embedding and output matrices of size V x d_model, plus the output softmax) or buys (fewer tokens per text, better coverage of scripts). The two-column table is one slide; 'Yi 64000' is listed under monolingual despite exceeding 50k, and the lecture does not comment. Spoken evidence (56:12-56:28): the professor adds a second driver the slide omits: scaling-law studies find larger models can use larger vocabularies, and the multilingual column is also the column of bigger models ('No ones training large monolingual models anymore'), so coverage and scale are confounded in p47. Q&A (56:48-57:10): multimodal models that tokenize images usually add a separate image tokenizer with its own large vocabulary. The question that followed, about comparing models across tokenizers, is the spoken-only KP bpb-tokenizer-comparison.

misconceptions.why_wrong: p47 splits the trend by language coverage, not date: monolingual models stay at 30-50k (LLaMA 32000 is newer than GPT-2's 50257) and only multilingual/production systems go to 100-250k. 'Monolingual vocabs don't need to be huge.'

knowledge_points.label: Compare models across tokenizers in bits per byte, not per-token perplexity
knowledge_points.statement: Per-token loss or perplexity cannot be compared across models with different tokenizers, because a token covers a different amount of text. Bits per byte can be compared (total log-loss in bits on a fixed text divided by its number of bytes), provided each tokenizer is complete, encoding the whole string without dropping anything, since every model is then scored on the same string with the same normaliser.

anchors.quote: language modeling is a generative modeling task. ... We are modeling the probability of a sequence. ... And you provide a probability over all strings, that's always valid to compare.

did you touch the sequence at all? ... they would drop some tokens or drop some words. ... That makes the comparisons invalid. ... But modern tokenizers are complete. ... for bits per byte, you're always normalizing with the same number, which is the number of bytes.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only. Bits per byte is not in the slides. It comes from a student question after the vocabulary slide (p47), which the professor calls 'not a hyperparameter question' (57:25). The captions lose most of the question ('How valid is it to compare bits?'), and the answer (57:30-58:31) gives two conditions: the tokenizer must not touch the sequence, and the normaliser must be the same (bytes). A follow-up about perplexity and downstream performance (58:34-59:15) ended unresolved ('I'm not sure I understand the question') and is not imported. The bytes-per-token arithmetic in the prompts is the author's.

prerequisites.note: Asked in the Q&A after the vocabulary-size slide (p47).

misconceptions.belief: The model with the lower per-token loss (or perplexity) is the better language model, whatever its tokenizer.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A per-token number is divided by the token count, which depends on the tokenizer. A tokenizer with shorter tokens produces more, easier tokens for the same text. Only a normaliser both models share, such as the byte count, makes the totals comparable.

misconceptions.belief: Bits per byte is always a valid comparison, whatever the tokenizer does.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only if the tokenizer is complete. A tokenizer that drops words or maps them to <unk> scores a different, shorter string, so its probability is not over the same text (58:04-58:14).

predict.q: Two models are scored on the same 1 MB of English text. Model A's tokenizer averages 4.0 bytes per token and its loss is 2.4 bits per token. Model B averages 3.0 bytes per token at 2.1 bits per token, so B has the lower per-token loss. What is B's loss in bits per byte?
predict.why: B: 2.1 bits/token ÷ 3.0 bytes/token = 0.70 bits per byte. A: 2.4 ÷ 4.0 = 0.60. A assigns the same text a higher probability (fewer total bits), so A is better even though B's per-token loss is lower. B's tokens are shorter, so each one is easier to predict.
predict.targets_misconception: The model with the lower per-token loss (or perplexity) is the better language model, whatever its tokenizer.

transfer.q: Two papers report perplexity on the same English test set: 8.0 with tokenizer X and 10.0 with tokenizer Y. What must you know about each tokenizer before you can say which model is better, and how would you then compare them?
transfer.answer: How many tokens each tokenizer produces for the test text (its bytes per token), and that neither tokenizer drops or alters text. Then convert to bits per byte: total bits = tokens x log2(perplexity), divided by the same byte count. The lower bits per byte wins.
transfer.why: Per-token perplexity is divided by a tokenizer-dependent count. The professor's two conditions are a complete tokenizer (nothing dropped) and a shared normaliser, the number of bytes (58:02-58:31).

transfer.invariant: compare the total log-probability of the same string under the same normaliser

knowledge_points.label: LLMs are 'regularised' with weight decay, but for optimisation, not overfitting
knowledge_points.statement: Pretraining sees trillions of tokens in a single pass, so overfitting is not the concern; older models used dropout 0.1 (original transformer, GPT-2/3, T5, OPT) while newer ones (except Qwen) use no dropout and only weight decay around 0.1 (GPT-2/3 0.1, LLaMA 0.1), and Andriushchenko et al. 2023 show weight decay's effect is through optimisation dynamics and its interaction with the cosine learning-rate schedule, not through controlling overfitting.

anchors.quote: Do we need regularization during pretraining? Arguments against: There is a lot of data (trillions of tokens), more than parameters. SGD only does a single pass on a corpus (hard to memorize)

Original transformer 0.1 0 ... GPT2 0.1 0.1 ... GPT3 0.1 0.1 ... T5 v1.1 0 0 ... PaLM 0 (variable) ... OPT 0.1 0.1 ... LLaMA 0 0.1 ... Qwen 14B 0.1 0.1 ... Many older models used ... dropout during pretraining ... Newer models (except Qwen) rely ... only on weight decay
[Andriushchenko et al 2023] has interesting observations about LLM weight decay. It's not to control overfitting. Weight decay interacts with learning rates (cosine schedule)
Regularization: You still 'regularize' LMs but its effects are primarily on optimization dynamics

So I'm only going to do a single pass on a corpus. ... So this means overfitting is not really a problem, almost ever during compute constrained language modeling. ... some people even actually only look at training loss

the stronger weight decay runs, these blue dashed lines on the bottom do significantly better, because they start out slow, but they essentially end up converging to a much better minimum later. ... generally true when we decay learning rate, not necessarily true when we're in constant learning rate

I don't think people do dropout anymore, because it doesn't really interact well with optimization. ... weight decay, which is shrinkage to 0, that might allow you to use a higher learning rate, or it might allow you to decay faster.
Weight decay, people change in concert with learning rate. ... That is actually a heuristic that people do.

knowledge_points.label: z-loss keeps the output softmax normaliser near 1
knowledge_points.statement: Softmaxes are a main source of instability because of exponentials and division by (near) zero; the z-loss adds a penalty on log Z, the log of the output softmax's normaliser, pushing log Z toward 0 so the final logits stay in a well-behaved range (from Devlin 2014, used by PaLM, Baichuan 2, DCLM, OLMo 2, OLMo 3).

anchors.quote: Where do the issues arise? Beware of softmaxes! Softmaxes - can be ill-behaved due to exponentials / divison by zero

Output softmax stability - the 'z-loss'. Recall the softmax calculation [From Devlin 2014]. This is useful for stability! PaLM used this 'z loss' trick. Other examples: Baichuan 2 (2023), DCLM (2024), OLMo 2 (2025), OLMo 3 (2025)
Recently, lots of attention on stable training. Don't train models that look like the blue curve!

the softmax has two things that are both really bad for stability-- one of them is an exponential. ... You also divide two numbers. ... There's one on the output side, when we output our probability distribution. ... And then in attention
This u is well-behaved ... Now, the second term, this log z, this might not be so OK. ... Now, we would ideally like our z to be somewhere near 1 or log z to be somewhere near 0.

this whole thing is overparametrized. ... if I add a constant to you, I can manipulate the z's without really affecting the output of the softmax. ... he adds this squared log z term. ... it's just penalizing how far away your log z is from 0.

provenance.filtering_note: The z-loss formula on p54 (the softmax, log Z, and the penalty alpha * log^2 Z) is an image with no text layer; the coefficient PaLM used (1e-4) is not on the slide and is taken from the PaLM paper anchor. The p52 loss-spike figure ('blue curve') carries no numbers. The lecture states that the penalty 'is useful for stability' without arguing why a normaliser near 1 helps (log Z near 0 bounds the magnitude of the logits that feed the exponentials). Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above: it says the lecture asserts 'useful for stability' without arguing why, but the professor argues it aloud (1:07:22-1:08:55). The log-probability is u - log Z; u is the residual-stream output and well behaved, while log Z can blow up in either direction (Z huge or near 0). Because the softmax is over-parametrised (adding a constant to every logit leaves the probabilities unchanged), log Z can be pinned near 0 at no cost, so the penalty is the squared log Z, which he says aloud while the formula is an image. He names Baichuan as the first open model to use it, then DCLM and OLMo (1:09:12-1:09:23). His 'Jacob Devlin's paper, 2024-- sorry, 2014' (1:08:40) is self-corrected.

misconceptions.belief: z-loss is a regulariser that improves perplexity like weight decay.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p54 presents it as a stability trick for the output softmax: it penalises log Z (the log normaliser) so that the softmax is nearly self-normalised and its exponentials do not blow up. Any quality effect is incidental; the slide's section is titled 'Stability tricks'.

predict.q: The z-loss penalises log Z, where Z is the softmax normaliser sum_i exp(z_i). Toward which value does the penalty push log Z?
predict.why: The penalty is alpha * (log Z)^2 (PaLM), minimised at log Z = 0, i.e. Z = 1: the unnormalised exponentials already sum to one, so the logits cannot drift to huge magnitudes.
predict.targets_misconception: z-loss is a regulariser that improves perplexity like weight decay.

transfer.q: A training run's final-layer logits drift upward over time until exp overflows in bf16 and the loss spikes. Name the trick from slide 54 that targets this, and say which quantity it constrains.
transfer.answer: The z-loss: it adds a penalty on log Z (the log of the output softmax's normaliser), keeping the logit scale from drifting so the exponentials stay finite.
transfer.why: p53 locates instabilities in softmaxes ('exponentials / division by zero'); p54 applies the penalty to the output softmax specifically.

check.q: The output logits over a 4-token vocabulary are [5, 5, 5, 5]. You subtract 5 from every logit. What happens to the z-loss penalty (log Z)², where Z = Σ exp(z_i)? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: down: log Z falls from 5 + ln 4 ≈ 6.39 to ln 4 ≈ 1.39, so the penalty falls from about 40.8 to about 1.9; the softmax probabilities stay at 1/4.
check.why: The z-loss pushes log Z toward 0 and is blind to the probabilities, since softmax is shift-invariant. Shifting the logits toward a scale where Z ≈ 1 is exactly what it rewards, which keeps exp() in a safe range (p53-p54).
check.targets_misconception: z-loss is a regulariser that improves perplexity like weight decay.
check.varies: a logit shift with probabilities held fixed, instead of naming the trick for a drift
check.invariant: z-loss penalises the scale of the logits (log Z), not their relative values

retrieval.answer: Softmaxes, because of exponentials (overflow) and division by zero (vanishing normaliser).

knowledge_points.label: QK-norm: normalise queries and keys before the attention softmax
knowledge_points.statement: QK-norm applies a LayerNorm/RMSNorm to the query and key vectors before their dot product enters the attention softmax, bounding the attention logits so the second softmax in the network cannot blow up; it came from vision and multimodal models (ViT-22B, Idefics, Chameleon) and is now used by DCLM, OLMo 2, Gemma 2, Qwen 3, OLMo 3 and Gemma 4.

anchors.quote: Attention softmax stability – the 'QK norm' ... The query and keys are Layer (RMS) normed before going into the softmax operation. ... Other examples: DCLM, OLMo2, Gemma 2, Qwen3, OLMo 3, Gemma 4 ... Originally from vision and multimodal models [Dehgani 2023, Idefcs, Chameleon]
Trends over the years (QK-norm, Hybrid attention)
if you have instability, if you can throw a layer norm in there, somehow, it might control it. ... And that's really, in some sense, the design philosophy behind this idea called the QK norm.

what happens if we just throw in a LayerNorm before we multiply the Qs and Ks? ... They're always going to have a scale of roughly one, because we've used the RMSE norm to divide the size of those Qs and Ks.

QK norm is actually a very standard intervention that most of the large models now introduce. ... It doesn't seem to affect performance from lots of different training runs, but it does definitely prevent the kinds of attention degeneracies.
And QK norm is here. ... And it does slightly better due to the fact that you can crank up the learning rate a little bit.

provenance.filtering_note: p55's figure is an equation image showing the norms inside the attention score; the text layer names the operation only. The lecture does not say whether the norm has a learned gain, whether it is per-head, or how it interacts with the 1/sqrt(d_k) scale; ViT-22B's motivation (uncontrolled growth of attention logits leading to near one-hot attention and divergence) is not stated on the slide. Spoken evidence (1:11:28-1:11:43, 1:13:14-1:13:28): QK-norm 'doesn't seem to affect performance' across many runs, and in the systematic comparison of stability interventions he attributes to 'some NVIDIA folks' (paper not named; not on the slides) it does slightly better than the baseline 'due to the fact that you can crank up the learning rate a little bit'. He frames it as the 'throw a layer norm in there' heuristic (1:09:48-1:10:04; see non-residual-double-norm) and says it keeps the attention logits at a scale of roughly one (1:10:31-1:10:55). Still not said: learned gain, per-head application, interaction with 1/sqrt(d_k).

prerequisites.note: p53's 'beware of softmaxes' covers both; z-loss handles the output softmax, QK-norm the attention softmax.
The norm applied to Q and K is the same RMSNorm/LayerNorm.

misconceptions.belief: QK-norm is the pre-norm of the attention block applied to its input.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Pre-norm acts on the block input x before the projections; QK-norm acts on the projected queries and keys (after W_Q and W_K) immediately before the dot product, so it bounds the attention logits themselves (p55: 'normed before going into the softmax operation').

predict.q: q and k are each RMS-normalised to unit RMS over head_dim d = 128 (no learned gain). What is the largest possible value of |q·k| / sqrt(d)?
predict.why: Unit RMS over 128 entries means ||q|| = ||k|| = sqrt(128); Cauchy-Schwarz gives |q·k| <= 128, so |q·k|/sqrt(128) <= sqrt(128) = 11.31. Without QK-norm the projected q and k can grow without limit and so can the attention logit; with it the logit is bounded (scaled by any learned gain).
predict.targets_misconception: QK-norm is the pre-norm of the attention block applied to its input.

transfer.why: p53 distinguishes the two softmaxes; p54 (z-loss) is the output one, p55 (QK-norm) is the attention one.
