knowledge_points.label: Logit soft-capping with tanh
knowledge_points.statement: Soft-capping replaces a logit z by c * tanh(z / c), which squashes every logit smoothly into (-c, c) so logits cannot blow up, at the possible cost of some performance; it is a third softmax-side stability trick alongside z-loss and QK-norm.

anchors.quote: Logit soft-capping. Soft-capping the logits to some maximum value via Tanh. Prevents logits from blowing up, but also might have perf issues?

this one is not as popular and more of a Google-specific trick ... in QK norm, what we're doing is we are controlling the inputs to the softmax and hoping that the outputs are well-behaved. ... we can just cap them off, so they can never be too large or too small.
this is in the Gemma models. ... I think Gemma 2, 3, and 4 all use the logit soft cap trick. ... they take all of their logits for the attention layers, and then they soft cap them at some value.

if you do soft-capping alone, you actually end up losing performance. ... So there is a quality degradation that happens. ... You can never express very confident signals in your softmax beyond a certain point.

provenance.filtering_note: The formula c * tanh(z / c) and any cap values are not in the slide text (the slide shows the formula as an image and names no model); the values 50 (attention) and 30 (final logits) come from the Gemma 2 anchor. The 'perf issues' remark is a question on the slide, not a result; the lecture does not say which models dropped soft-capping (Gemma 3 replaced it with QK-norm, not on the slides). Spoken evidence, which answers the slide's open question: p56 asks whether soft-capping 'might have perf issues?', and the professor answers yes. In the comparison he attributes to NVIDIA researchers, 'soft-capping alone' loses performance, because 'you can never express very confident signals in your softmax beyond a certain point' (1:13:28-1:13:41). He contrasts it with QK-norm: QK-norm controls the softmax inputs and hopes the outputs behave, soft-capping caps the logits directly, 'almost a hard constraint' (1:12:21-1:12:45). He calls it 'more of a Google-specific trick' and names the Gemma models, applied to the attention logits (1:12:51-1:13:08). Spoken slip (likely), not imported: 'I think Gemma 2, 3, and 4 all use the logit soft cap trick' (1:12:54). The Gemma 3 report says soft-capping was replaced by QK-norm (see the note above). He also says 'outputs of your attention-- or sorry, the inputs' (1:13:41), self-corrected.

misconceptions.belief: Soft-capping is the same as clipping the logits at ±c.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Clipping has zero gradient beyond the cap and a kink at it; c * tanh(z / c) is smooth, approximately identity for |z| << c, and approaches ±c asymptotically while keeping a nonzero gradient everywhere, which is why it is 'soft'.

predict.q: With soft-cap c = 50, a raw logit of 200 becomes approximately what value?
predict.why: 50 * tanh(200 / 50) = 50 * tanh(4) ≈ 50 * 0.99933 ≈ 49.97. The logit is pulled just under the cap rather than cut off at exactly 50, and still has a small gradient.
predict.targets_misconception: Soft-capping is the same as clipping the logits at ±c.

transfer.q: With cap c = 30, compare what happens to a logit of 3 and a logit of 300 under soft-capping, and explain what that means for the softmax probabilities over tokens whose raw logits are 300 and 600.
transfer.answer: 3 -> 30 tanh(0.1) ≈ 2.99 (nearly unchanged); 300 -> 30 tanh(10) ≈ 30 (saturated). Both 300 and 600 map to ≈ 30, so the softmax can no longer separate them: that compression is the 'perf issues' concern on slide 56.
transfer.why: tanh is identity near 0 and flat far from it; extreme logits lose their ordering, which bounds the softmax input at the cost of expressiveness at the top.

check.targets_misconception: Soft-capping is the same as clipping the logits at ±c.
check.varies: a different cap and logits; asks how much separation survives
check.invariant: c·tanh(z/c) is near identity for small z and saturates toward c for large z

retrieval.answer: c * tanh(z / c), mapping into (-c, c).

retrieval.q: What downside of soft-capping does the lecture raise?
retrieval.answer: It might have performance (quality) issues.

knowledge_points.label: MQA/GQA: share K and V across heads to fix incremental-decoding arithmetic intensity
knowledge_points.statement: During parallel training, attention's arithmetic intensity is high (O(1/k + 1/(bn))^-1), but during step-by-step generation with a KV cache the per-step intensity is O(n/d + 1/b)^-1, dominated by reading the cache; multi-query attention keeps h query heads but a single key/value head, shrinking the cache term to n/(d h), and grouped-query attention uses a few KV heads as a knob between expressiveness and inference cost, with a small perplexity hit for MQA (Shazeer 2019) and little or none for GQA (Ainslie 2023).

anchors.quote: Let's think about the compute involved for attention ... d = hidden dim ... b = batch ... n = length (<d) ... h = heads ... k = head dim (d/h) ... Total arithmetric operations ... total memory accesses ... Arithmetic intensity (compute/memory) is high ... we can keep our GPUs running

What's the incremental arithmetic intensity? ... Total arithmetric operations ... total memory accesses ... Arithmetic intensity is not good ... need large batches + short seq length ... (n) or big model dimensions (d) ... Is there some way around this? The n/d term is difficult to reduce.

misconceptions.belief: MQA/GQA save compute, which is why they speed up inference.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The arithmetic operations on p60 and p61 are the same (b n d^2); what changes is memory accesses, because the KV cache that must be re-read every step shrinks from h heads to 1 (MQA) or a few (GQA). The win is arithmetic intensity, i.e. bytes moved, not FLOPs.

predict.q: A model has 32 query heads of dim 128 and uses GQA with 8 KV heads. By what factor is its KV cache smaller than with full multi-head attention?
predict.why: The cache stores K and V per KV head: 32 / 8 = 4 times fewer. MQA (1 KV head) would give 32x; p62 calls the KV-head count the 'simple knob' between expressiveness and inference efficiency.
predict.targets_misconception: MQA/GQA save compute, which is why they speed up inference.

transfer.q: Incremental decoding intensity is O(n/d + 1/b)^-1 (slide 60). For a fixed model, name the two things slide 60 says you can change to raise it, and say which of them MQA attacks and how its expression changes.
transfer.answer: Use larger batches (shrinks 1/b) and shorter sequences (shrinks n/d); 'big model dimensions' is the model-side lever. MQA attacks the n/d term, turning it into n/(d h) by storing one KV head instead of h.
transfer.why: p60: 'need large batches + short seq length (n) or big model dimensions (d) ... The n/d term is difficult to reduce'; p61 shows the MQA expression O(1/d + n/(dh) + 1/b)^-1.

check.q: A model switches from multi-head attention to multi-query attention, keeping all h query heads but storing one shared K/V head. At a fixed context length and batch, what happens to the attention-score FLOPs (the q·k dot products) per decoded token? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: same: every query head still takes a dot product with each of the n cached keys; what falls is the bytes of K and V read from the cache.
check.why: MQA attacks the memory term: the n/d cache-read term becomes n/(d h) (p60-p61) because one K/V head is read instead of h. The number of query-key products is unchanged, so the gain comes from arithmetic intensity, not from fewer FLOPs.
check.targets_misconception: MQA/GQA save compute, which is why they speed up inference.
check.varies: asks about compute instead of the memory term MQA shrinks
check.invariant: MQA/GQA reduce K/V bytes per decode step, not the query-key FLOPs

retrieval.q: Why does arithmetic intensity drop in incremental (generation) attention compared with training-time attention?
retrieval.answer: Generation is step by step and must re-read the KV cache of n previous tokens each step, so memory accesses grow (b n^2 d) while the arithmetic stays b n d^2; intensity falls to O(n/d + 1/b)^-1.

retrieval.q: What is the structural difference between MQA and GQA?
retrieval.answer: MQA: many query heads, one shared key/value head. GQA: a few key/value heads, each shared by a group of query heads (a knob between MHA and MQA).

retrieval.q: What quality cost does the lecture report for MQA and for GQA?
retrieval.answer: MQA: a small perplexity hit (Shazeer 2019); GQA: low to no hit (Ainslie 2023).

prompts.self_explain: Why does sharing K and V across heads reduce memory traffic in decoding but barely change the FLOPs?

steps.do: Training, all n positions at once (p58): arithmetic bnd², memory bnd + bhn² + d².
steps.why: Divide each memory term into the arithmetic. With k = d/h and n < d, the first two terms are each at most 1/k, so intensity is high and the GPU stays busy.

steps.do: Generation, one token per step (p59-p60): over n steps the arithmetic is still bnd², but every step re-reads the KV cache (b·n·d) and the weights (d²), so memory is bn²d + nd².
steps.why: Steps cannot run in parallel, so the cache is read n times instead of once and the weights are re-read at every step.

steps.do: Divide.
steps.why: The cache term n/d is new and does not shrink with batch size; it is what makes decoding memory-bound.

knowledge_points.label: Sparse / sliding-window attention interleaved with full attention
knowledge_points.statement: Full attention is quadratic in context length, so models restrict the pattern (sparse/strided as in Child et al. 2019 and GPT-3, sliding-window as in Mistral and GPT-OSS); the current standard is to interleave local and full layers, e.g. Cohere Command A makes every 4th layer full attention and uses NoPE in full layers for long-range information and RoPE plus SWA in local layers, while LLaMA 4, Gemma 3/4 and OLMo 3 do SWA plus full attention with RoPE.

anchors.quote: Attending to the entire context can be expensive (quadratic). Build sparse / structured attention that trades off expressiveness vs runtime (GPT3, GPT-OSS, Gemma4) [Child et al 2019]

Current standard trick - interleave 'full' and 'LR' attention. From Cohere Command A - Every 4th layer is a full attention. Long-range info via NoPE, short-range info via RoPE + SWA. Other models - LLaMA 4, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, OLMo 3 does SWA+Full RoPE.
Sparse or sliding window attention (GPT4/Mistral): restricting the attention pattern to reduce compute cost. Exotic SSM stuff (Jamba, Falcon 3, Qwen 3.5, etc): next lecture!

if you read the paper, they'll say, we alternate between full attention, where every position can attend to everyone in the past, and a banded matrix style attention, where you can attend to everyone within a fixed window.

Cohere Command A was the first one I saw do it, where they had this structure, where every four layers, they would have a full attention that attended to everything. ... The three layers in between would use a sliding window attention

people change the embedding format for the long range information, where they get rid of things like RoPE. ... So you have no position embeddings at all. ... So you're really looking, almost, at bags, where the short range information still gets position information.
Qwen3.5, which I've put on the right, they're actually a little bit different, because they alternate a state space model called gated delta net and one full attention for every four layers.

'LR' on p65 means long-range. 'NoPE' (no position embedding in the full-attention layers) is used without definition. Hybrid SSM/attention models (p57, p66 Qwen 3.5) are deferred to the next lecture. Spoken evidence, which corrects the note above: it says 'NoPE' is used without definition, but the professor defines it aloud: the long-range layers 'get rid of things like RoPE ... no position embeddings at all', so they see the context 'almost, at bags', while the short-range layers keep position information (1:26:46-1:27:02). Also spoken: GPT-3 already alternated full and banded attention (1:25:14-1:25:30); Command A's pattern is one full layer followed by three sliding-window layers (1:25:57-1:26:17); Qwen 3.5 replaces the cheap layers with a Gated DeltaNet state-space layer, explained next lecture (1:27:48-1:28:15); and long-context attention is 'still an active area of investigation' (1:27:13-1:27:29). How local layers come to use global information is the spoken-only KP swa-reach-through-depth.

prerequisites.note: The NoPE vs RoPE split on p65 presumes the taxonomy of p30.

misconceptions.belief: Sliding-window attention replaces full attention everywhere in a modern model.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p65: the 'current standard trick' interleaves local and full layers; in Command A every 4th layer is full attention so long-range information still has a path. All-local would cap the receptive field at window x depth.

predict.q: Command A makes every 4th layer full attention (slide 65). In a 64-layer model, how many layers are sliding-window (local)?
predict.why: 64 / 4 = 16 full-attention layers; the remaining 48 are local SWA layers. Three quarters of the attention compute is window-bounded, one quarter remains quadratic.
predict.targets_misconception: Sliding-window attention replaces full attention everywhere in a modern model.

transfer.q: Per slide 65, Command A gives the full-attention layers no position embedding (NoPE) and the local layers RoPE + SWA. Give the design reason for assigning the position embedding this way, using the p30/p31 taxonomy.
transfer.answer: Local layers only see a short window, where relative position (RoPE) is informative and cheap to encode; the full layers handle long-range retrieval, where imposing RoPE's distance-dependent structure is less useful and NoPE lets attention depend on content alone. The slide's wording: 'Long-range info via NoPE, short-range info via RoPE + SWA.'
transfer.why: RoPE makes scores depend on i - j (p31), which is the right inductive bias within a window; for arbitrary-distance lookups the model relies on content.

check.q: A model interleaves sliding-window layers (window 4,096 tokens) with full-attention layers, Command A style. A fact 50,000 tokens earlier must be retrieved. Which layers can attend to it directly?
choices: every layer, each via its window
distractor_from: 'no layer at that distance' <- misconception: 'Sliding-window attention replaces full attention everywhere in a modern model.'
'every layer, each via its window' <- plausible: confuses multi-layer receptive-field growth with direct attention
'only the sliding-window layers' <- plausible: reverses the split of long- and short-range roles
check.why: A sliding-window layer sees only the last 4,096 positions. Long-range information goes through the full layers, which is why Command A gives them NoPE (content-only lookup) and keeps RoPE for the local layers: 'Long-range info via NoPE, short-range info via RoPE + SWA' (p65).
check.targets_misconception: Sliding-window attention replaces full attention everywhere in a modern model.
check.varies: a retrieval distance instead of the position-embedding assignment
check.invariant: local layers handle short range, full layers carry long-range information

retrieval.answer: Full attention over the context is quadratic in sequence length.

knowledge_points.label: Local attention layers reach past their window through depth
knowledge_points.statement: A sliding-window layer attends only within its window, but its input already carries what earlier layers gathered. In an interleaved stack the full-attention layers write long-range information into the residual stream, so later local layers 'can access more global information'. Even a stack of only local layers reaches about (layers x window) tokens back, while each layer pays only window-sized attention cost.

anchors.quote: as you go down these blocks, you're aggregating local information into global ones. ... So the local attentions at the end can, of course, access more global information, but this allows you to manage the cost of having a really long context
This idea of alternating the big, full attention and a more local attention actually hits a sweet spot for how to manage long context performance while not paying too much for inference.
From Cohere Command A – Every 4th layer is a full attention

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken for the mechanism. Slide p65 gives Command A's layout ('Every 4th layer is a full attention') and p64 the cost motivation, but no slide says how the local layers come to use long-range information. The professor says it while pointing at Command A's diagram (1:26:17-1:26:44; 'down, because they ordered the diagram the other way'). The reach of a stack of only local layers (about layers x window) extends the same mechanism and is the author's, used in the transfer and check. The ~131K figure is from the Mistral 7B paper, not the lecture. Reach is an upper bound on what can flow, not evidence that a model uses it.

misconceptions.belief: A sliding-window layer's output can only depend on tokens inside its window.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Its input is the residual stream, which already mixes in what earlier layers attended to. A full-attention layer below, or a chain of local layers, carries information from far outside the window.

misconceptions.belief: Stacking more sliding-window layers does not extend how far back the model can see; only a larger window does.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each local layer can move information up to one window further back, so reach grows with depth: k layers of window w reach about k x w tokens.

predict.q: In a Command A style stack, layer 4 is full attention and layer 5 is sliding-window attention with a 4,096-token window. Can the output of layer 5 at position 60,000 depend on the token at position 1,000?
choices: Yes, through what layer 4 wrote into its input
No, layer 5 only sees the last 4,096 tokens
Only if layer 5 uses NoPE instead of RoPE
Only at inference time, via the KV cache
predict.answer: Yes, through what layer 4 wrote into its input
distractor_from: 'No, layer 5 only sees the last 4,096 tokens' <- misconception: 'A sliding-window layer's output can only depend on tokens inside its window.'
'Only if layer 5 uses NoPE instead of RoPE' <- plausible: confuses the position-embedding choice with what the layer can attend to
'Only at inference time, via the KV cache' <- plausible: the KV cache stores past keys but does not widen the window
predict.why: Layer 5 attends only to roughly the last 4,096 positions, but each of their residual vectors already includes layer 4's full-attention output, which can draw on position 1,000. The professor: 'the local attentions at the end can, of course, access more global information' (1:26:17-1:26:44).
predict.targets_misconception: A sliding-window layer's output can only depend on tokens inside its window.

transfer.q: A model uses only sliding-window attention (no full layers), with a 4,096-token window in all 32 layers. Roughly how many tokens back can information reach the top layer's output? Type only the number.
transfer.why: Each layer can move information up to one window back, so 32 x 4096 ≈ 131,072 tokens (the Mistral 7B paper quotes this ~131K 'theoretical attention span'; not in the lecture). The window bounds each layer's cost, not the stack's reach.
transfer.targets_misconception: Stacking more sliding-window layers does not extend how far back the model can see; only a larger window does.
transfer.varies: a stack of only local layers, asking for the total reach
transfer.invariant: each local layer extends reach by at most one window

check.q: With a 2,048-token sliding window and no full-attention layers, what is the smallest number of stacked layers after which the top layer's output can depend on a token about 16,000 positions back? Type only the number.
check.why: Each layer extends reach by about one window: 16,000 / 2,048 ≈ 7.8, so 8 layers (7 layers reach only about 14,300).
check.varies: solving for depth instead of reach, with a different window
check.invariant: reach ≈ number of local layers x window

retrieval.q: If a sliding-window layer sees only its window, how can a local layer late in an interleaved stack use information from far away?
retrieval.answer: Its input residual stream already contains what earlier layers attended to, including the full-attention layers below, so global information arrives through depth.

retrieval.q: How far back can information travel through k stacked sliding-window layers with window w?
retrieval.answer: About k x w tokens, one window per layer.
